parsing_res_list.block_content: Then  $ \Phi(z) $ is called a root function of  $ Q(z) $ of order at least m at the critical point (or zero)  $ \alpha $. If m is the maximal number for which condition (b) holds, then  $ \Phi(z) $ is said to be a root function of exact order (or exact partial multiplicity) m at  $ \alpha $.

The vector  $ \Phi(\alpha) $ is called an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue  $ \alpha $. If  $ \Phi(z) $ is a root function of maximal order m among all root functions with the same eigenvector  $ \Phi(\alpha) $, then  $ \Phi(z) $ is called a canonical root function associated with  $ \Phi(\alpha) $. The sum of the orders of all linearly independent canonical root functions at  $ \alpha $ is called the (total) multiplicity of the zero at  $ \alpha $.
The maximal order among all canonical root functions at  $ \alpha $ is called the order of the zero at  $ \alpha $.

Pole cancellation functions are closely related to root functions. They were introduced and extensively studied in the investigation of an important subclass of operator-valued functions, namely generalized Nevanlinna functions; see, for example, [3,4].

Definition 1.2. Let  $ Q : \mathcal{D}(Q) \to \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}) $ be an operator-valued function holomorphic on  $ \mathcal{D}(Q) $. Suppose that the vector functions  $ \hat{\Phi}(z) $ and  $ \Psi(z) $ satisfy the following conditions at a pole  $ \beta \in \mathbb{C} $ of  $ Q $:
(b)  $ \Psi^{(l)}(z) \to 0 $ as  $ z \to \beta $, for  $ 0 \leq l \leq m - 1 $, where  $ l, m - 1 \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\} $.

The functions  $ \hat{\Phi}(z) $ and  $ \Psi(z) $ are called a pole function and a pole cancellation function, respectively, of  $ Q(z) $ at  $ \beta $ of order at least m. If m is the maximal number for which condition (b) holds for a given vector  $ \hat{\Phi}(\beta) $, then  $ \hat{\Phi}(z) $ and  $ \Psi(z) $ are called the pole function and the pole cancellation function, respectively, of  $ Q(z) $ at  $ \beta $ of exact order m.

If  $ \Psi(z) $ is a pole cancellation function of maximal order  $ m $ among all pole cancellation functions associated with the same limit  $ \hat{\Phi}(\beta) $, then  $ \Psi(z) $ is called the canonical pole cancellation function associated with the vector  $ \Phi(\beta) $. The sum of the orders of all linearly independent canonical pole cancellation functions at  $ \beta $ is called the (total) multiplicity of the pole at  $ \beta $.
The maximal order among all canonical pole cancellation functions at β coincides with the order of the pole at β.

By definition,  $ \beta = \infty $ is a pole (respectively, a zero) of Q if and only if 0 is a pole (respectively, a zero) of  $ G(\zeta) := Q(1/\zeta) $. Hence, all of the preceding definitions and considerations extend naturally to the pole  $ \beta = \infty $ of Q via the function  $ G(\zeta) $ at  $ \zeta = 0 $.
